title: NVIDIA BlueField-4 Powers New Scale-In Network Infrastructure for Agentic AI Factories | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA declares 'Scale-In' the fifth pillar of its AI networking taxonomy — alongside Scale-Up, Scale-Out, Scale-Across and Context Memory — and positions BlueField-4 DPUs plus DOCA software as the mandatory infrastructure processor for north-south access, security, storage and control-plane operations in agentic AI factories. BlueField-4 brings a 64-core Grace CPU with 6x its predecessor's compute, 800 Gb/s line-rate inline acceleration, PCIe Gen6, and 4x the memory bandwidth of BlueField-3, and doubles as the data processor for the new CMX KV-cache storage tier.

insights.claim: NVIDIA is creating a fifth networking category — Scale-In — that turns north-south datacenter access into a co-designed, accelerated infrastructure domain built on BlueField-4, DOCA and Spectrum-X Ethernet.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Each new 'pillar' NVIDIA names is a new attach-rate line per GPU server; Scale-In converts what was commodity NIC and host-CPU work into NVIDIA silicon content.
insights.quote: NVIDIA is introducing Scale-In network infrastructure, the fifth pillar of NVIDIA AI networking, bringing purpose-built acceleration to secure, manage, and operate agentic AI factories.
insights.locator: Traditional cloud infrastructure was designed for predictable

insights.claim: The full stack is now segmented as Scale-Up (NVLink), Scale-Out (Spectrum-X Ethernet and Quantum InfiniBand), Scale-Across (Spectrum-XGS Ethernet), Context Memory (CMX on the STX modular foundation), and Scale-In (BlueField-4 plus DOCA).
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: A map of every interconnect socket NVIDIA now claims; useful for identifying which merchant-silicon and storage vendors are being designed out at each layer.
insights.locator: AI factories have distinct infrastructure requirements at different scales

insights.claim: NVIDIA's core argument is that scaling GPUs and racks delivers no value unless data access, storage, cybersecurity and operations scale with them — the justification for making a DPU mandatory rather than optional per server.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: If the DPU becomes a required component of every AI server rather than a hyperscaler-only option, DPU attach rate is a second, under-modeled growth vector alongside GPU units.
insights.quote: Scaling GPUs, racks, and data centers delivers value only when data access, storage, cybersecurity, and operations scale with them.
insights.locator: Together, these five infrastructure pillars address distinct requirements

insights.claim: BlueField-4 is dual-purposed — it is the infrastructure processor for Scale-In and, separately, the data and storage processor for CMX, the pod-level shared KV-cache tier — so each AI factory needs BlueField silicon in more than one role.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Two distinct sockets per deployment materially raises BlueField unit volumes independent of GPU count — model DPU attach at greater than 1x per server.
insights.quote: BlueField-4 serves as the infrastructure processor for Scale-In and, separately, as the data and storage processor for CMX.
insights.locator: AI factories rely on complementary storage infrastructures

insights.claim: BlueField-4 pairs a 64-core Grace CPU running policy, provisioning, telemetry and orchestration software with inline acceleration engines that process packets, RDMA, storage protocols, encryption and firewall rules at up to 800 Gb/s.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: A 64-core Grace CPU inside the NIC is effectively a second server per node — meaningful incremental silicon content and power draw per AI server.

insights.claim: The BlueField-4 Grace CPU provides 6x more compute than its predecessor, enabling multiple infrastructure services to run concurrently on the DPU rather than sequentially.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Concurrency on the DPU is what lets third-party security and observability vendors ship as DOCA microservices — an emerging software ecosystem to watch.
insights.quote: Provides 6x more compute than its predecessor, enabling multiple infrastructure services to run concurrently

insights.claim: Against BlueField-3, BlueField-4 delivers 4x more memory bandwidth and 2x more network bandwidth, with an LPDDR5X memory subsystem, a PCIe Gen6 host connection and an 800 Gb/s network interface.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: PCIe Gen6 and LPDDR5X in the DPU pull forward demand for those component generations across the server supply chain, not just in the GPU itself.
insights.quote: Compared with BlueField-3, BlueField-4 provides 4x more memory bandwidth and 2x more network bandwidth.

insights.claim: In Vera Rubin NVL72 the roles are split: ConnectX-9 SuperNICs carry tenant workload traffic on the Scale-Out network while BlueField-4 runs infrastructure services in a separate processing domain outside the tenant host.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Two distinct NVIDIA network ASICs per compute tray — ConnectX-9 and BlueField-4 — is the concrete networking BOM for the Rubin generation.
insights.locator: BlueField-4 accelerates Scale-In services across GPU servers

insights.claim: Vera Rubin's coordinated policy model spans 7.2 Tb/s of aggregate interface bandwidth per compute tray — 800 Gb/s north-south through BlueField-4 plus four 1.6 Tb/s east-west paths — so east-west traffic never funnels through the 800 Gb/s interface.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: 7.2 Tb/s per tray is a hard number for sizing optics, cabling and switch port demand per Rubin rack.
insights.quote: In Vera Rubin, this coordinated model spans 7.2 Tb/s of aggregate interface bandwidth, comprising 800 Gb/s on the north-south BlueField-4 path and four 1.6 Tb/s east-west paths per compute tray.
insights.locator: Build isolated AI factory virtual private clouds

insights.claim: BlueField-4 places the security enforcement point in hardware outside the host operating system, so tenant software cannot disable or bypass network, file and object access controls — a structurally different trust model from host-resident security agents.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Directly threatens host-agent security vendors in AI datacenters; the defensible position for them becomes shipping as DOCA microservices rather than host software.
insights.quote: Tenant software cannot disable or bypass these controls, while offloaded security processing preserves host CPU cycles and avoids a separate software hop.

insights.claim: NVIDIA now ships named security services on the DPU — DOCA Argus for runtime threat detection, DOCA Vault for file-access policy, and DOCA Flow for line-rate network enforcement — moving from silicon vendor into the security software stack.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Watch for margin mix shift as NVIDIA attaches software services to networking silicon, and for competitive response from incumbent security vendors.

insights.claim: BlueField Astra creates a closed control loop across both network domains — BlueField-4 installs policies and monitors telemetry while ConnectX-9 enforces them directly in the data path — keeping privileged control outside tenant hosts.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Astra is the lock-in mechanism: a unified policy model only works if both the DPU and the SuperNIC are NVIDIA parts.
insights.quote: BlueField-4 installs and updates policies and monitors telemetry, while ConnectX-9 enforces those policies directly in the data path.
insights.locator: NVIDIA BlueField Astra extends trusted control

themes.theme: Storage path as the new GPU stall risk

insights.claim: The stated failure mode is that GPUs sit idle waiting for data whenever storage protocol processing, storage virtualization or data movement cannot keep pace — even when compute and Scale-Up/Scale-Out bandwidth are available.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Storage-side bottlenecks are the least-modeled source of GPU underutilization; it is the argument driving AI-native storage refresh cycles.
insights.quote: If storage protocol processing, storage virtualization, or data movement cannot keep pace, GPUs wait for data despite having available compute and Scale-Up/Scale-Out network bandwidth.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims the co-designed BlueField-4 plus Spectrum-X Ethernet storage path delivers up to 1.45x more storage throughput than off-the-shelf Ethernet, with BlueField-4 offloading NVMe-oF, file and object protocols over both RDMA and TCP.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: A 1.45x storage throughput claim is the wedge NVIDIA uses to sell Spectrum-X into the storage network, a segment historically held by commodity Ethernet.
insights.quote: up to 1.45x more storage throughput than off-the-shelf Ethernet

insights.claim: DOCA Platform Framework is a Kubernetes-native orchestration layer that provisions and scales BlueField DPUs as Kubernetes nodes, handling discovery, service deployment and updates across the AI factory.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Making DPUs first-class Kubernetes nodes embeds NVIDIA in the orchestration layer operators already run — high switching cost once deployed.
insights.quote: DOCA Platform Framework is a Kubernetes-native orchestration framework that provisions, manages, and scales BlueField DPUs as Kubernetes nodes.
insights.locator: Run the AI factory control plane

insights.claim: BlueField-4 runs the AI factory control plane independently of the host — onboarding nodes, provisioning networking and storage, starting servers and loading the host OS over the network before tenant software ever boots.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Owning pre-boot provisioning is the deepest form of platform control; it shortens time-to-capacity, which is the operator metric that justifies the DPU premium.
insights.locator: Run the AI factory control plane

insights.claim: DOCA Telemetry gives operators fleet-wide visibility into network, storage, service health and utilization that is independent of tenant-host software, and third-party observability providers can integrate the same signals through DOCA libraries.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Host-independent telemetry is a data moat: the operator's ground truth about utilization flows through NVIDIA silicon.

insights.claim: BlueField-4 uses multiservice architecture with native service function chaining to route each traffic flow through the required sequence of services, replacing separately managed per-server software pipelines.
insights.speaker: Ronil Prasad
insights.so_what: Service chaining in hardware is what makes DPU-hosted third-party services viable — the enabling condition for a DOCA microservice marketplace.
